response.complaint_restatement: Sasha claims that Ellis’s specific promise places her in a qualitatively distinct position: once assured the blanket, she holds a defeasible right that cannot be outweighed by merely a 20-percentage-point survival gap. Therefore the principle that permits Ellis to break the promise (PR_MaxProb) is reasonably rejectable.
conceded_points: A broken promise adds a morally significant burden both to Sasha (betrayal) and to Ellis (breach of integrity).
Promises can generate special obligations that are more than just another cost to be balanced against impersonal benefits.
If Rowan’s and Sasha’s survival prospects were equal, the pre-existing promise would tip the balance decisively toward Sasha.
response.priority_premise: P1 Under contractualism, a principle is reasonably rejectable when at least one affected party can point to a substantially greater ex ante loss that others could not reasonably object to avoiding (N1).
response.answer: The special status created by a promise does not give the promisee an absolute veto; it must still be assessed against the life-and-death stakes of the other affected individual. From Rowan’s standpoint, Principle PR_KeepPromise exposes her to a 100 % risk of death she could otherwise avoid with an 80 % prospect of survival. She can reasonably say: “I face certain death for the sake of preserving an assurance I never benefited from.” By contrast, under PR_MaxProb Sasha faces (i) a 40 % lower survival prospect and (ii) betrayal. The betrayal is grave, but not as grave as forfeiting one’s only chance at life; reasonable persons would foresee that life-or-death rescues may override pre-discovery promises when new victims appear with higher need. Hence PR_KeepPromise is more reasonably rejectable than PR_MaxProb, and the blanket should still go to Rowan, though Ellis owes Sasha regret, explanation, and compensatory apology.
response.countercomplaint_to_alternative: If Ellis honors the promise (Action B) Rowan can reasonably protest that PR_KeepPromise singles her out for certain death despite an available blanket that would give her a significantly higher chance to live, merely because Ellis spoke too soon. That imposition is not one she must reasonably accept when a less objectionable principle (PR_MaxProb) exists.
response.comparative_justification: Both principles impose betrayal on someone: PR_MaxProb betrays Sasha; PR_KeepPromise in effect betrays Rowan’s legitimate expectation that life-saving aid will not be denied for avoidable reasons. The magnitude of betrayal-plus-life-loss is greater for Rowan under PR_KeepPromise (certain death) than for Sasha under PR_MaxProb (40 % higher death risk). Therefore PR_MaxProb remains the less reasonably rejectable principle.
